Israel's Minister of Foreign Affairs Gideon Saar has said that UK-Israeli relations have been "damaged" following a "series of unilateral anti-Israel measures pursued by the Labour government since 2024".

Saar made the comments following a meeting with a visting delegation from the British Conservative Party on Wednesday evening in Jerusalem.

In a post on X, he said he had briefed the group "on the strategic challenges facing Israel, including the ongoing, systematic and openly declared attempt by Iran and its allies to destroy it".

But he warned that the relationship between Israel and the UK has been damaged "against our wishes", and said that "attempts to harm Israel also harm Britain itself".

I was pleased to meet this evening in Jerusalem with a visiting delegation from the British Conservative Party, led by Party Chairman Kevin Hollinrake. I briefed our friends on the strategic challenges facing Israel, including the ongoing, systematic and openly declared attempt by Iran and its allies to destroy it. The relationship between Israel and Britain is important to both countries. Unfortunately, it has been damaged, against our wishes, by a series of unilateral anti-Israel measures pursued by the Labour government since 2024. As attorneys general from 13 U.S. states recently warned, attempts to harm Israel also harm Britain itself. Israel still has good friends in Britain, and I thanked them for standing with Israel! 🇮🇱🇬🇧 @CFoI @kevinhollinrake @A_J_Snowden @AWMurrison @drcarolinej @JeromeMayhew @gavinantonyrice

articles.title: Former Mossad officer’s appointment highlights Tel Aviv University’s military ties
articles.summary:
Former Mossad officer’s appointment highlights Tel Aviv University’s military ties

Submitted by Nadav Rapaport on Thu, 11/12/2026 - 11:44
University appoints ex-intelligence official to senior role as it prepares to host a defence technology conference sponsored by major Israeli and US arms companies
A view of the cyber horse sculpture made of recycled computers outside Tel Aviv University campus, Israel 5 June 2023 (Reuters/Amir Cohen)
Off

A former senior Mossad officer’s appointment as Tel Aviv University’s vice-president for industry relations and entrepreneurship has been seen as another sign of the university’s close ties to Israel’s defence establishment, Local Call reported on Tuesday.

According to the report, the university (TAU) announced last month that Hagai Itkin, a former officer in Israel’s foreign intelligence agency, had been appointed to the role based on his previous experience, including “senior positions in the defence establishment”.

The university added that Itkin had held positions on campus for several years before his appointment, building “connections and links with the high-tech industry”.

Itkin retired from the Mossad in 2020 after nearly 20 years of service. 

In 2022, he told Israel’s Channel 12 News that he had worked in the agency’s technology department in the years leading up to his retirement.

“The State of Israel has all the capabilities required to carry out targeted assassinations,” Itkin said when asked about alleged Israeli assassinations of Iranian scientists. 

He added that Israel carries out assassinations “while giving maximum consideration to collateral damage and to innocent people”.

Universities' military ties

Meanwhile, TAU will host the “DefenseTech Week” conference next month for the second consecutive year, further strengthening its links with the defence establishment, according to Local Call.

The university described the December event as “a premier gathering for experts in defence technology”, showcasing “Israel’s cutting-edge solutions that are addressing global security challenges”.

The conference website said Israel was ideally placed to host the event because it was “at the forefront of defence technology development”. It added that the conference would offer “invaluable insights into how Israel’s advancements are shaping the global defence landscape”.

TAU is co-organising the event with the Directorate of Defence Research and Development at Israel’s Defence Ministry. Israeli and US arms companies are among its sponsors.

'Israeli academia often adopted militaristic rhetoric and continued to cooperate in various ways with the military, Israel’s security establishment, and the arms industry'

- New Profile, Israeli NGO

Shield AI, a US-based defence technology company developing autonomous pilots, is one of 22 sponsors. Others include Israel’s three major arms manufacturers - Rafael, Elbit and Israel Aerospace Industries - as well as US defence giant Lockheed Martin.

Speakers include senior military and defence ministry officials, former US Army officers, arms industry executives and academics from Israel and the US.

Local Call said that by appointing Itkin and hosting the conference, TAU “inevitably takes a stand on the connection between war, weapons, and business”. It accused the university of ignoring the use of Israeli arms industry products to suppress, expel and kill Palestinians in the occupied territories.

The university’s efforts to strengthen its ties with the Israeli defence establishment, the report added, “reflect a deep and ongoing ideological, political, and economic line of Israel’s universities”.

 The close relationship between Israeli universities and the military is not new.

According to New Profile, an Israeli NGO dedicated to demilitarising Israeli society, Israeli academic institutions remained silent during the genocide in Gaza, as Israel committed war crimes and crimes against humanity.

“Worse, Israeli academia often adopted militaristic rhetoric and continued to cooperate in various ways with the military, Israel’s security establishment, and the arms industry,” the group said last April.

Middle East Eye has previously reported that TAU boasted of helping to develop live dog cameras for the Israeli army’s canine unit. An academic at the university also called for Gaza’s population to be starved and exterminated.

articles.title: 'Mighty US' must talk with Iran, Iraqi Kurdish leader says
articles.summary:
'Mighty US' must talk with Iran, Iraqi Kurdish leader says

Submitted by Sean Mathews on Thu, 11/12/2026 - 09:19
Bafel Talabani, leader of the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan, also said Iran promised it was not behind attack on Iraqi gas field
Bafel Talabani in Tehran, Iran, on 16 September 2026 (Zuma Press Wire via Reuters)
Off

The US needs to stop treating Iran as if it is governed by "mad mullahs" and engage in dialogue with the Islamic Republic, which is emerging "stronger but different" from the US-Israeli war, a senior Iraqi Kurdish official said on Thursday.

"Iranians are often misunderstood in the West. This notion of mad mullahs is far from the truth," Bafel Talabani said at a Strategic Forum in the Iraqi Kurdistan city of Sulaymaniyah.

"We don't find it difficult talking to the Iranians," he said. "As an ally of Mr Trump and, strangely, an ally of the Iranians [I say] the mighty US can do it," he added.

Talabani leads the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK), which is the dominant political party in southeastern Iraqi Kurdistan.

The PUK's administrative zone accounts for most of the region's long border with Iran.

The PUK has historically enjoyed close ties to Tehran, but that relationship came under strain earlier this year after US President Donald Trump and his advisers tried to recruit Talabani and other Kurdish leaders to support a Kurdish insurgency in Iran.

Talabani eventually decided not to intervene.

Iraqi Kurds suggest peace process between Iran and Iranian Kurdish opposition
Read More »

A senior Kurdish official in Sulaymaniyah told Middle East Eye that the PUK warned Iranian opposition groups against launching attacks on Iran at the time, saying they were sure to fail. 

Tehran has been pressuring Iraqi Kurdistan to clamp down on Iranian Kurdish opposition groups. In a meeting in September with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, Talabani promised not to allow Iraqi Kurdistan to become "a haven for harming or threatening" the Islamic Republic.

Talabani said that Iran was emerging from the US-Israeli war "stronger, but different". Recounting a recent trip he made to Iran, he offered a very different assessment to that proposed by members of the Trump administration who have characterised Iran as on the verge of economic collapse.

"I thought I was in London," Talabani said, noting that "less then 50 percent of ladies and girls had scarves" and that restaurants were filled with young people dancing.

Iran not behind attack on Khor Mor gasfield

Iran launched strikes on Iranian opposition groups in Iraqi Kurdistan following the US-Israeli attack in February 2026.

Talabani was asked about a drone strike earlier this week on the Khor Mor gas field in the Sulaymaniyah Governorate.

'The timing and methodology of the attack [on Khor Mor] needs to be investigated very seriously'

– Bafel Talabani, leader of the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan

The field, operated by a UAE company, is one of the largest in Iraq and the strike has left almost 70 percent of Kurdistan without normal power supplies.

Talabani said he asked Iranian officials pointedly if they were behind the attack and he was assured they were not.

"Iran has guaranteed me that it was not by their bidding or doing," he said. "The timing and methodology of the attack needs to be investigated very seriously." 

Iraqi Kurdistan has no air defence systems. The last US troops left Erbil, the region's capital, in September, completing a full US withdrawal from Iraq.

Some US lawmakers have since tried to advance the sale of air defence systems to Iraqi Kurdistan, but Talabani said that the semi-autonomous region was in a "grey area".

"There is a 'one Iraq' policy and the majority of these things need to happen with the OK of Baghdad," he said. "Either provide us with certain systems, or allow us to purchase our own. We are in a grey area."

Kurdish rift

Talabani spoke at a time when Iraq's semi-autonomous Kurdish region is reeling from a major internal political rift.

Talabani withdrew his PUK, one of the two main political parties in the Kurdistan Regional Government, from the region's parliament this week.

The PUK has traditionally been a rival of the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP), which is led by the region’s president, Nechirvan Barzani.

Talabani called the rift the "single largest political crisis in the history of the Kurdistan region", saying that the region effectively had "two administrations".

The US envoy to Iraq and Syria, Tom Barrack, weighed into the rift, which has raised fears about a splintering of the province at a time of uncertainty over the region's security framework.

"The Barzanis, the Talabanis, have always been great friends of America. This is an Iraqi issue," Barrack said. "My advice is get over it."

War on Iran
